newsitem.title: USA: In tobacco country, worry and anger greet settlement.
newsitem.headline: In tobacco country, worry and anger greet settlement.

text.p: In the heart of tobacco growing country in North Carolina, growers, sellers and others in the industry reacted with a mixture of worry, anger and sarcasm to Friday's historic tobacco settlement.

"I've said all along, give us the rules, tell us how to play the game, then leave us alone," said David Stephenson, of Lumberton, who sold more than 12 million pounds of the leaf out of his warehouse in 1996.
"Let me tell you something, though. These state attorney generals (sic) aren't interested in protecting children from smoking. They want the almighty dollar."

Under the tentative agreement announced in Washington, the tobacco industry agreed to pay $368.5 billion over 25 years to help states recoup tax money spent treating ill smokers. The industry also would admit to the ill-effects of smoking and accept federal regulation of their products and advertising.
Stephenson said he and most other tobacco farmers he knows agree that children should be shielded from tobacco products and advertising.
"But don't feed us out of a different spoon than the other vices," he said. "I've never heard of anyone killed from drunk smoking, have you?"
He said the issue could have been solved years ago when states first began to file suit against the tobacco industry -- by taking drastic action to make them back off.

"Every tobacco product should have been pulled from every shelf ... the politicians would have seen how much income they were losing from tobacco taxes," he said. "Sometimes you have to fight fire with fire."
Tobacco is a critical crop in North Carolina, Virginia, Kentucky and other southern U.S. states. It is the sixth or seventh most valuable crop grown in the United States.
In North Carolina's Robeson County alone, it generated $51.1 million in sales last year.
Farm receipts for tobacco will reach about $3 billion this year in the 17 or 18 U.S. states where it is grown, according to a University of Kentucky professor.
Barnesville resident Newberry Mitchell, 68, has been growing tobacco for 35 years, but said the agreement could mean the end of a way of life.
"How are tobacco farmers supposed to live?" he asked, the bitterness evident in his voice.
"The government's going to take tobacco away from us, but they aren't going to give us anything back."
William Graham of Proctorville, a retired loan officer with Farm Credit Services, said he wanted to see how Congress would protect tobacco growers.
"That's when we'll know where we stand in all this," he said.

Everett Davis, director of the Robeson County Cooperative Extension Service in Lumberton, said many tobacco farmers would find adapting difficult if they had to stop producing the leaf and grow something else.
"It's not like they can just switch from tobacco to tomatoes or other vegetables," he said.
"Even if they could, the demand for vegetables would soon be saturated. The farmers will need time to adjust."
Earlier this month North Carolina lawyer Phil Carlton, representing tobacco companies at a Raleigh, N.C. meeting, assured growers' representatives that farmers will not be forgotten.
Members of the U.S. House and Senate from tobacco states have also vowed to protect farmers' interests as the settlement is reviewed by Congress.
